title: Hunt Instead of Wait: Evaluating Deep Data Research on Large Language Models
one_liner: This paper evaluates whether an agent can open a database, decide what to inspect, and discover useful findings without being handed a narrow question.
lead: Many benchmarks ask an agent to answer a stated question. Real data work often starts earlier: open the data, decide what is worth checking, and then discover the questions that matter. This paper studies that earlier stage and treats it as a separate form of agent capability.

problem.h2: Answering a stated question is easier than deciding what to investigate in the first place
paras: A standard benchmark usually gives the agent a clear prompt and asks for a correct answer. That setup tests execution once the goal is already known. It does not test whether the agent can inspect raw data, notice promising directions, and choose what to examine next.

Data analysis is a useful setting for this harder test because real analysts often begin with tables and logs rather than with a single narrow question. The paper asks how to evaluate an agent that must decide where to look, what to compare, and which findings deserve follow-up.

callout.html: Benchmark open-ended data investigation directly, because a capable agent should not only execute a stated task but also decide what is worth exploring.

panels.title: 1. The agent opens raw data
panels.viz_args: No single target question is provided at the start.
panels.caption: The task begins with data inspection rather than with a narrow answer request.

panels.title: 2. Many possible directions appear
panels.viz_args: Different tables, fields, and time windows could matter.
panels.caption: The agent must choose what to inspect because the search space is broad.

panels.title: 3. The agent hunts for signals
panels.caption: The system explores, compares, and revises its focus based on what the data reveals.

panels.title: 4. Findings are checked against a checklist
panels.viz_args: The benchmark asks whether the discovered findings match known important insights.
panels.caption: Evaluation stays verifiable because the benchmark has a structured checklist.

panels.title: 5. The score reflects investigatory ability
panels.viz_args: Credit depends on what the agent discovered, not only on how well it executed a single prompt.
panels.caption: The benchmark targets autonomous exploration rather than prompt following alone.

steps.b: Give the agent raw data access
steps.text: Start from databases or tables without supplying one narrow analysis question.

steps.b: Let the agent choose exploration steps
steps.text: Allow it to inspect columns, compare slices of data, and pose follow-up checks based on what it finds so that its next move depends on evidence from the previous move.
Capture the insights and evidence the agent produces during its exploration.
Score whether the important discoveries were found so that open-ended exploration remains measurable.
Use the benchmark to separate plain task execution from autonomous discovery.

paras: The paper changes the benchmark target. Instead of asking only whether the agent can answer a question, it asks whether the agent can decide which questions deserve investigation inside raw data.
object.object: the benchmarked definition of agent competence

hidden.name: how well the agent chooses worthwhile directions before a final question is fixed
paras: The paper distinguishes execution from investigation. Execution means carrying out a known task once the goal is set. Investigation means choosing promising directions when the goal is still under discovery.

This hidden quantity matters because a system can follow instructions well and still fail at open-ended analysis. Without a benchmark for investigatory intelligence, progress can look stronger than it really is on real data work, since fixed-question tests hide the earlier choice of what to inspect.

heat.caption: The darkest cells mark the parts of analysis where the agent must choose its own direction instead of waiting for a narrow prompt.

reads.html: A useful data agent must know where to look before it knows exactly what answer it will give.
Investigatory intelligence captures autonomous direction choice, which means the benchmark evaluates a capability that standard question-answer settings mostly skip.

mechanism.h2: Why this benchmark reveals something new
paras: The benchmark reveals something new because it removes the narrow task prompt that normally anchors the agent's search. Once that anchor is removed, the system must supply its own exploration strategy.

The checklist-based evaluation keeps the task measurable because open-ended analysis still needs a way to compare runs. By defining important findings in advance, the benchmark can score discovery quality without forcing every agent to follow the same exploration path.

stages.s: Raw database with no fixed narrow question
Agent chooses its first probes and comparisons
Agent follows evidence toward useful findings
Checklist scores which important findings were reached

math.words: Investigatory score grows when the agent finds more key insights and wastes fewer exploration steps on dead ends.
symbols: how well the agent performs on open-ended data investigation
how many of the benchmark's important findings the agent discovers
how much exploration effort is spent on unhelpful directions

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the benchmark has 10 important findings and the agent discovers 7, so insight_coverage is 7.
Suppose the run also spends effort on 2 major dead ends, so dead_end_cost is 2.
Then investigatory_score is 7 minus 2, which is 5.
A second agent that also finds 7 insights but wastes no major detours would score 7 instead.
The example shows why exploration quality matters because finding insights is only part of the job.

math.note: This simple difference is only a teaching view. The benchmark's point is that autonomous discovery and disciplined search both matter.

charts.title: Prompt-following agent
charts.note: A system can execute well after a question is given and still struggle when it must decide what to inspect first.

charts.title: Investigatory agent
charts.note: The benchmark values this profile because it shows the ability to hunt through the data rather than wait for an exact prompt.

items.html: Open-ended exploration can drift toward eye-catching but unimportant differences, so the run burns time without producing a key benchmark finding.
If the benchmark checklist omits a genuinely valuable discovery, an agent may do useful work that the score does not recognize.

items.b: The agent never commits to a direction.
items.html: A system that keeps sampling many views of the data without deepening any one line of inquiry can appear active while making little progress.
The setup works when the benchmark rewards real discoveries and the agent is forced to balance breadth of exploration with enough depth to verify an insight.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark with raw databases from sales, health, or operations domains. For each database, define a checklist of high-value findings that a good analyst should uncover. Let agents inspect the data freely, record their probes and conclusions, and then score both discovered findings and wasted exploratory detours.

The demo proves the paper's point if agents that look strong on fixed-question tasks still miss many checklist findings here, because the open-ended setting requires a separate capability: choosing what to investigate.
demo.closing: A convincing result should show one case where an agent answers prompted questions well but fails to notice the main story when no question is supplied.
